issues.legal_issue: A trust administered and situated principally outside a state is not deemed registered under that state’s public-trust law merely because some of its property lies there, and therefore cannot obtain a land-tenancy exemption certificate on that basis.
material_facts: The appellant headed a public and religious trust registered under the public-trust law of another state.
The trust was administered outside Maharashtra, and most of its property was situated there.
Only three pieces of the trust’s land were in Maharashtra, including land tenanted by the first respondent.
The appellant sought an exemption certificate so that the tenant would not be deemed to have purchased the land.
issues.conclusion: The trust was not deemed registered under the Bombay Public Trusts Act and did not satisfy the registration condition for an exemption certificate. The appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 88B(1)(b) and its proviso of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, a trust seeking the exemption must be or be deemed registered under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, in addition to satisfying the other stated conditions; a certificate under section 88B(2) is available only if those conditions are met. Section 28 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, read with Schedule AA added by the Bombay Public Trusts (Unification and Amendment) Act, 1960, deems trusts registered under the Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951 to be registered under the Bombay Act when they have come within Maharashtra as a result of territorial reorganisation. It does not extend that status to a trust that remains administered outside Maharashtra merely because some of its property is in Maharashtra. The Acts do not contemplate dividing a trust’s administration between the two states. Without the required deemed registration, the trust cannot obtain the section 88B certificate that would prevent the tenant from being deemed a purchaser under section 32. No earlier cases are relied on.
